summary:
Our Project LunarX features-

• 14 real Artemis south-pole landing sites, with Sun + Earth positions computed from a from-scratch ephemeris (reproduces 8 reference values to ≤0.004°) • Verdicts per site per hour: POWER (SUNLIT / LOW SUN / DARK) and COMM (VISIBLE / BELOW HORIZON) — now terrain-aware, from real LOLA DEM horizons (range 9,990 m). No at-horizon model remains. .9-point gap, shown as-is, not tuned • Honest validation shown in the app: computed 80.2% Sun-up vs published 88.1% (Gläser 2014) — a 7 • Real LRO LOLA DEM terrain under the rover (10 m/px for 10 sites, 20 m/px for 3); real LROC NAC imagery at 8 sites • Real Apollo LRV model from NASA's Space ROS project (GitHub space-ros/simulation PR #32, Deutsches Museum model, CCBYSA 4.0 — attribution is in the app). WASD/arrows + Space brake, 5–18 km/h, chase + driver cameras, live HUD. • Sun-path chart in the Evidence modal; full data sources in app/SOURCES.md • Stated limits (in the app): "planning aid only, not for ight decisions"; kinematic rover physics, at smooth-sphere terrain beyond the DEM tile, decorative rocks, no collision
details:
LunarX compares 14 real Artemis Moon south-pole landing sites by where the Sun and Earth sit relative to each site's real horizon, for any date and hour the user picks. For every site it answers the two questions that decide whether a landing can work: POWER — is the site sunlit, low-sun, or dark (solar power)? And COMM — is Earth above the horizon (direct-to-Earth radio) or below it?

How it works: instead of a flat-horizon approximation, the app computes a terrain-aware horizon for each site from real LRO LOLA elevation data (range 9,990 m), then runs a from-scratch ephemeris — Sun position, Earth position, lunar libration — reproduced against 8 published reference values to within 0.004°. The verdicts update live as the user drags the date and time, and a Sun-path chart in the Evidence view shows the Sun's track across the sky for the chosen site and date.

The second half is Drive mode: the user drives a real Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle across real LRO terrain — a 1.2 km square heightfield built from LOLA DEM (10 m/px for 10 sites, 20 m/px for 3), with up to 130 m of relief at Malapert Massif, real LROC NAC imagery on 8 sites, WASD/arrows plus Space brake, 5–18 km/h, chase and driver cameras, and a live HUD. The rover is the real Apollo LRV: the Deutsches Museum model from NASA's Space ROS project, converted to GLB, decimated from 375,237 to 97,340 triangles and scaled to the published 3.1 m length, 1.83 m track and 0.818 m wheels (CC-BY-SA 4.0, attribution in the app).

Benefits and intended impact: mission planners currently juggle separate ephemeris tools, terrain maps and lighting studies. This puts power and comms windows for all candidate sites in one interactive view, honest about its limits — it is labelled "planning aid only, not for flight decisions", and its one validation gap is shown in the open: computed 80.2% Sun-up vs 88.1% published (Gläser 2014), a 7.9-point difference we did not tune away. For students and the public, the rover makes the same data tangible — you drive the terrain the verdicts are computed from.

Tools and languages: JavaScript (Vite + React 19 + Tailwind v4), three.js (plain three, no react-three-fiber), Node/npm, Vitest (202/202 tests passing), Blender (DAE-to-GLB conversion), GitHub Pages hosting. Data: NASA LRO LOLA DEM, LROC NAC imagery, published Apollo LRV dimensions (NSSDCA), Gläser et al. 2014 illumination data. No hardware was used — the whole project runs in the browser.

What makes it creative: the project turns a planning problem into something you can drive. The same terrain model feeds both the engineering verdicts and the rover experience — the numbers and the drive agree with each other. And the honesty is deliberate: the app shows its own validation gap instead of hiding it.

Factors the team considered: accuracy first (real DEM, real ephemeris, verified against published values); honest limits (the flat-horizon model was replaced, not patched; "planning aid only" label); licensing (all data and the rover model are openly licensed and attributed); accessibility (runs in any browser, no install); and performance (the rover model and textures were decimated and compressed so the app stays fast on a normal laptop).
